column2: Metamorphosis (after M.C. Escher's woodcut strip "Metamorphosis II", which is itself a long 2:1 band). The glass is a living tessellation that scrolls slowly and continuously: a regular tiling of interlocking creatures (birds becoming fish becoming lizards, or a tiling of your own invention) whose tiles deform smoothly along the strip, so one creature morphs into the next as it travels. The numerals emerge out of the tiling itself: the tiles inside a digit's shape are a contrasting colour family (or the digit is where the tiling flips figure/ground), so the time is the pattern, not a font pasted on it; design all ten as tile-made shapes with clean silhouettes. Constant 60 fps life: the scroll, the creatures' eyes and fins, the morph wave. Minute turn: a metamorphosis wave sweeps through the changing digit: its tiles morph into the other creature, flip, and re-tile into the new digit. Hour: a bigger, distinct show (the whole strip morphs into a different tiling or palette; a lizard crawls out of the plane as in Escher's "Reptiles" and back in). Palette: woodcut-like, few flat colours with crisp keylines, hard pixels where it helps. Precompute the tiling into buffers; per-pixel shape tests over the whole glass will blow the budget.

The illuminated manuscript. The glass is a page of a medieval book of hours on vellum: the numerals are historiated initials, designed as a set of ten, with gold leaf that glints as a candle flame moves (the gold must catch light as the light moves), lapis blue and vermilion grounds, white filigree, vine scrolls and tiny figures living inside the counters (a snail in the 0, a knight climbing the 1, a bird nesting in the 8, grotesques in the margins). Always alive at 60 fps: the candlelight flickers and sweeps the gold, margin creatures (a rabbit with a sword, a snail duel) act out little scenes, a vine grows. Minute turn: a scribe's quill (or a monk's hand) scrapes the old initial off the vellum with a knife, then lays the new one in stages: gold leaf burnished first, then the colour fills, then the filigree drawn line by line; the time is never wrong. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. a page turn revealing a new spread, with the time readable through it. Small text, if any, in a blackletter / Gothic textura you draw yourself. Night: candle only, warm and low.

The abyss. The deep ocean at 3,000 m: deliberate deep-blue darkness (not flat black: the water itself has a faint gradient and drifting marine snow at several depths, parallax), and the only light is bioluminescence. The numerals are made of living light: a shoal of lanternfish or a colony siphonophore whose photophores form the digits, or the glowing lures of anglerfish, or comb jellies whose rainbow cilia ripple along their bodies. Design all ten digits as living light shapes that stay readable. Always alive at 60 fps: pulsing photophores, comb-row rainbows running along bodies, marine snow, an anglerfish drifting with its esca swinging. Minute turn: something hunts or startles: the old digit's lights flash in alarm (a burglar-alarm display) and scatter into the dark, then a new shoal gathers and lights up as the new digit. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. a giant squid or a submersible with floodlights passes, its beam sweeping and briefly revealing the real shapes, or a vampire squid inverts. Use additive glow; colours of real bioluminescence (blue-cyan mostly, a few red/green species). Night is natural here; make day subtly different (e.g. faint blue light from above at noon).

A match-3 puzzle game, live. The glass is a candy/gem board (an 8-row grid fits the 2:1 strip at ~10 px cells, or choose your own) of glossy faceted gems in 5-6 colours with specular sparkles at 60 fps, idle wobbles and an occasional hint glow. The time is spelled by the board: the gems that form each digit are one special kind (e.g. gold or rainbow gems, or a contrasting glowing outline), so the numerals are made of the game's pieces, laid out on the grid; design all ten as cell patterns that read well. An invisible player keeps making moves around the digits (swaps, small matches, cascades, falling refills), so the board is always alive without ever breaking the digits. Minute turn: a combo chain: the old digit's gems are matched and explode in a flash and particles, the column cascades down, and the new digit's gems fall into place from the top with bounce; the time is never wrong. Hour: a bigger show (a special bomb or colour-bomb wipes the board in a wave and refills it with the new time, a "LEVEL UP" banner). A score in a game-style font you draw is welcome as clearly secondary detail. Bold, saturated colours, clean shapes.

The topiary garden. A formal garden in a strip panorama (gravel paths, a stone balustrade, a fountain, a sky that follows the day): the numerals are clipped box/yew hedges, sculpted, with leafy texture, shaded volume and cast shadows, designed as a set of ten hedge shapes (a 0 a hedge arch, an 8 two stacked balls, etc.). A gardener character (bold, 16+ px, clear) with big shears or a ladder works the hedges all the time; birds land, leaves rustle in a breeze at 60 fps. Minute turn: the hedge physically becomes the new digit: the gardener clips away the parts that are not in the new digit (clippings fly), and the parts the new digit needs grow out in a fast-forward leafy burst; time is never wrong (clip first before :00, grow after). Hour: a bigger show, e.g. a crew of gardeners, a hedge-trimmer race, or the fountain jets in a show. Night: lanterns along the path, moonlit hedges that still read.

The painted cave. A rock wall deep in a cave lit by a moving torch: uneven stone with bumps and cracks that the light rakes across, ochre, charcoal and red-iron paints, handprint stencils. The numerals are painted animals (aurochs, horses, deer, ibex, mammoths, bison) drawn in the Lascaux style whose bodies, horns, legs and backs form each digit; design all ten so the animal is clear AND the digit reads (e.g. a bison curled as 0, a horse rearing as 7). Always alive at 60 fps: the torch flickers and the light pool drifts, so the painted animals seem to move (the real effect at Lascaux), dust in the beam, a smoke curl. Minute turn: a painter's hand blows pigment through a reed to stencil and paint the new animal stroke by stroke after the old one fades into the rock in the dark; the time is never wrong. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the herd runs along the wall in flickering firelight then settles into the new hour. Earthy palette of real pigments; the dark must be warm rock, not black.

Slot-car racing, top-down. The numerals ARE the race track: a slot-car track (grey asphalt with white lane edges, red-white kerbs, the two slots) whose layout traces each digit, with cars racing around the digits at 60 fps — this face shows off the high refresh. Design all ten digits as track layouts with real track pieces (straights, curves, a crossover where needed) that read clearly. Two or three cars, bold and bright, with lights, drift on corners, sometimes deslot and get put back by a hand. Pit, grandstand, a lap counter in a design-fitting font as secondary. Minute turn: a marshal's flag, the cars pull off, a giant hand lifts the changing digit's track pieces out and clicks in the new layout, then the cars rejoin; the time is never wrong. Hour: a bigger show (a chequered-flag finish with confetti, the cars racing a figure-eight across all digits). Watch tearing on fast horizontal motion; small cars moving fast are where 60 fps pays off.

A turn-based artillery game in the style of Worms. The numerals are islands of destructible terrain (grass on top, soil and rock strata below, hand-painted look) standing in water, designed as a set of ten landforms; little bold soldier worms (or your own characters, 12+ px, big eyes) live on them, crawl, idle, wear helmets, taunt. Always alive at 60 fps: waves, wind-blown clouds, a wind indicator, worms fidgeting, an occasional jetpack hop. Minute turn: the battle: a worm aims and fires a bazooka arc at the old digit; explosions blast craters that eat it away until it sinks (gone before :00); then the new island rises out of the water (or is airdropped as a landmass) and the worms parachute back on. Never a wrong digit: the craters must make the old digit unreadable, not read as another digit (e.g. sink it rather than leave a 3 that reads as 7). Hour: a bigger show (an airstrike, a banana bomb, a giant sheep) with the time readable. Team-coloured worms; a little HP number above a worm counts only as clearly secondary detail.
